title: Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale

paper.title: Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale
paper.abstract: Abstract Reusable skills let LLM agents load task-specific instructions on demand, but they make execution depend on implicit routing over skill metadata. We test whether this design scales by holding SkillsBench tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills. We find skill routing collapse : agents increasingly load fewer or no skills, even though the relevant skills remain available. With 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall falls from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%, whereas explicit selection from the same library retains 73.9% recall. Loading other skills, including plausible alternatives to golden skills, is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only the descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores skill loading, yet with the metadata intact, explicitly asking agents to plan skill use still yields lower recall than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task execution. We also evaluate explicit preselection as a practical mitigation, including its coverage and latency trade-offs. Our analysis informs skill protocols and evaluation for agents with growing skill libraries. 1 1 1 Code: https://github.com/jinlinll/lost-in-implicit-routing .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language model (LLM) agents now operate tools and files to complete multi-step workflows in software engineering, data analysis, document processing, and personal assistance ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Such agents need reusable procedures: a plotting routine, code-audit workflow, spreadsheet operation, or domain-specific calculation should not be rediscovered in every new task. Figure 1: Lost in implicit routing. The relevant skills remain installed, but as irrelevant skills grow, agents increasingly fail to load them during implicit execution. Explicit routing recovers much of the missing skill recall. Agent skills package such procedures and their supporting resources into reusable modules ( Anthropic, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and public skill libraries are growing quickly: one analysis reports 2,179 listed skills on January 16, 2026 and 40,285 on February 5 ( Ling et al., 2026 ) . Skill selection is therefore becoming a scaling problem. We use skills to mean Anthropic’s Agent Skills, whose progressive-disclosure design works as follows: the model first sees only skill names and descriptions, and opens a full skill file only if it judges the skill relevant ( Anthropic, 2026 ) . Routing is thus not a separate stage: the agent decides whether and which skills to load while planning actions, inspecting files, and solving the task. We call this execution-time selection implicit routing . It keeps long skill files out of context, but assumes that an agent can pick out the few relevant skills from many descriptions while simultaneously solving the task. We test this assumption on SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026 ) , which provides fixed task instructions, workspaces, verifiers, and relevant skills; for each task, we keep these fixed and vary only the number of added irrelevant skills. The result is skill routing collapse : the right skills are installed, but agents increasingly load fewer skills or none at all. As irrelevant skills grow from 0 to 1,000, loaded-skill recall under implicit routing drops from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%. Agents occasionally load non-golden alternatives, but too rarely to explain the collapse. Yet the same models retain 73.9% selected-skill recall when asked only to choose skills from the full library. Relevant skills thus remain recognizable; they are lost when routing becomes a subtask of execution. End-to-end Pass@3 falls less sharply, from 51.6% to 38.6%, because strong agents can sometimes solve around missing skills; task success alone can therefore make a failing skill system look healthy. We make three contributions: • We identify and measure skill routing collapse : growing libraries make agents load fewer or no skills, rather than substitute other skills for golden ones. • We compare LLM, retrieval, and hybrid preselection on libraries of up to 10,000 added skills, and derive scale-dependent recommendations together with their token, coverage, and latency costs. • We show that irrelevant descriptions suppress skill loading and that selecting skills while solving the task makes selection less reliable, revealing semantic and instruction interference beyond context growth alone. Figure 2: Overview of the controlled skill-scaling setup and routing strategies. Starting from an existing SkillsBench task, we keep the instruction, files, verifier, and relevant skills fixed while varying only the number of added irrelevant skills.

sections.heading: 2.1 Task setup
sections.text: We represent each task as τ = ( I , F , V , G ) \tau=(I,F,V,G) : instruction I I , workspace F F , executable verifier V V , and the set G G of relevant (golden) SkillsBench skills. A run succeeds only if V V passes after the agent finishes; no LLM judge is used. With s s added irrelevant skills, the installed library is S s = G ∪ D s S_{s}=G\cup D_{s} , where D s D_{s} is sampled independently of the task. Varying only s s tests whether an agent can still find and load the needed skills as the metadata list grows (Figure 2 ).

sections.heading: 2.2 Routing strategies
sections.text: Under implicit routing , the executor sees the metadata of all skills in S s S_{s} and decides during execution whether to open any skill. Explicit routing adds a preselection step: a preselector receives the task and the metadata and exposes only a compact subset to the executor, which still follows progressive disclosure and must open a skill before using it. We compare three preselectors. LLM preselection chooses directly from the full metadata list; RAG preselection retrieves skills by embedding similarity; and hybrid preselection retrieves candidates and lets an LLM make the final choice (pseudocode in Appendix K ). We also include a no-skill baseline.

sections.heading: Diagnosis versus mitigation.
sections.text: We use explicit routing in two ways. In routing-only diagnosis , the selector sees the task and the full library, including the same distractors as the executor, but only selects skills; selected-skill recall thus tests whether the needed skills are recognizable without task execution. In preselection-plus-execution , the executor then sees only the selected subset; loaded-skill recall and task success measure the practical benefit. The diagnosis changes only the objective, whereas the mitigation also narrows the executor’s library.

sections.heading: 2.3 Metrics
sections.text: Pass@3 is task success, computed with the standard unbiased estimator over repeated runs. Loaded-skill recall is | G ∩ L | / | G | |G\cap L|/|G| , where L L is the set of skills opened during execution; the zero-load rate is the percentage of runs with | L | = 0 |L|=0 , and average skills loaded is the mean of | L | |L| . For explicit routing, selected-skill recall is | G ∩ P | / | G | |G\cap P|/|G| , where P P is the preselected set. Appendix F reports precision, and Appendix I analyzes the loading of non-golden skills.

sections.heading: SkillsBench tasks.
sections.text: SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026 ) provides task instructions, workspace files, executable verifiers, and task-specific golden skills. We exclude five tasks with infrastructure or environment problems and use the remaining 82 (Appendices A and B ). Runs are costly: under implicit routing, one run averages 15.3 minutes and 485k input tokens without irrelevant skills, rising to 17.0 minutes and 1.95M input tokens with 1,000.

sections.heading: Skill libraries.
sections.text: We downloaded more than 20,000 skills from a skill market in leaderboard order and sample irrelevant skills from this pool with a fixed seed (42), so the distractors are identical across models and strategies. We evaluate s ∈ { 0 , 10 , 100 , 1000 , 10000 } s\in\{0,10,100,1000,10000\} , always installing the golden skills. Every preselector exposes at most five skills: LLM-based selectors choose up to five, and RAG returns the top five by embedding similarity.

sections.heading: Models and scale.
sections.text: Given this cost, the main experiments use three open-weight executors: GLM-5 ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , Kimi K2.5 ( Bai et al., 2026 ) , and MiniMax M2.5 ( MiniMax AI, 2026 ) ; RAG and hybrid preselection use Qwen text-embedding-v4 embeddings. Each model runs every task and condition three times, and we average over the task–model–run grid, for more than 15,000 trajectories and 10 billion tokens in total. A budget-limited validation on Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4 yields consistent conclusions (Appendix E ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Lost in Implicit Routing
sections.text: Figure 3: Implicit-routing scaling by execution model. (a) End-to-end Pass@3. (b) Loaded-skill recall. (c) Zero-load rate. Only the number of added irrelevant skills changes.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Implicit loading degrades before task success
sections.text: Figure 3 shows implicit routing for the three open-weight models. Implicit routing collapses as irrelevant skills grow. With only 100 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall already falls by 24.6, 15.6, and 20.7 points for GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and MiniMax M2.5 (Table 2 ), while zero-load rates rise: agents increasingly stop using skills at all rather than merely choosing wrong ones. Task success lags behind. At the same scale, GLM-5 keeps Pass@3 almost unchanged (57.3% to 56.1%) and Kimi K2.5 stays near its baseline (52.4% to 50.6%). Strong executors can solve around missing skills, so final success alone hides a failing skill protocol. Three proprietary models on a 37-task subset show the same pressure: Claude Opus 4.6, for example, keeps Pass@3 at 62.2% with 1,000 irrelevant skills (vs. 64.9%), yet its loaded-skill recall falls from 81.3% to 30.9% (Appendix E ). The collapse is also not confined to multi-skill tasks: at 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall falls from 91.9% to 38.0% on single-skill tasks and from 58.8% to 14.8% on tasks with four or more golden skills (Appendix G ). Appendix D.1 lists all plotted values.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Library growth suppresses skill use
sections.text: Table 1 shows that from zero to 1,000 distractors, the average number of loaded skills falls from 1.72 to 0.66 and the zero-load rate rises from 9.2% to 50.8%. Could agents instead be replacing golden skills with other skills? Non-golden loading is rare (2.32% of evaluations), and only 0.95% of evaluations load a non-golden skill whose embedding cosine similarity to a missed golden skill exceeds 0.8. Such loads concentrate at s = 1000 s=1000 (7.19% and 3.79%, respectively), and the above-threshold cases are near-duplicates such as pdf-reader for pdf or excel for xlsx . When agents do load skills, the loads are mostly correct: under implicit routing at 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill precision is still 88.6%, 87.2%, and 76.4% for the three models (Appendix F ). By construction, no distractor duplicates a golden skill. Routing collapse therefore primarily reflects under-loading, not substitution (details in Appendix I ). s s Avg. skills loaded ZeroLoad Load Rec. 0 1.72 9.2 73.5 10 1.54 13.0 67.8 100 1.20 27.9 52.9 1000 0.66 50.8 27.6 Table 1: Skill-loading behavior as the number of irrelevant skills grows. sections.heading: 3.2.3 The same skills are recognizable when selected explicitly
sections.text: Are the relevant skills intrinsically hard to recognize? Table 2 compares implicit loaded-skill recall with routing-only selected-skill recall for the same models and scales. The same LLMs still identify the needed skills when selection is explicit. At 1,000 irrelevant skills, GLM-5 loads 20.9% of golden skills but selects 82.5%, and Kimi K2.5 loads 40.5% but selects 80.7%; MiniMax M2.5 shows a smaller but still large gap (21.5% vs. 58.4%). The full metadata list thus often suffices for recognition when selection is the sole objective; the failure arises when selection is folded into reading files, planning commands, and completing the task. sections.heading: 3.3 Analyzing Explicit Routing
sections.text: Since the bottleneck lies in routing during execution, we next ask how much preselection helps when the executor sees only the selected subset. We do not propose a new routing algorithm; we compare simple preselectors to show when this design helps and what it costs.

sections.heading: Coverage and latency trade-offs.
sections.text: Fixed preselection can omit skills that become necessary later. As distractors grow from 10 to 1,000, the average number of golden skills exposed to the executor falls from 2.21 to 1.78 for LLM preselection, from 2.38 to 1.85 for RAG, and from 2.21 to 1.97 for hybrid preselection, compared with 2.52 when all golden skills are visible (Appendix J ). Coverage alone does not determine success: at 1,000, RAG exposes more golden skills than LLM preselection but reaches lower Pass@3 (46.5% vs. 51.6%), suggesting that which skills survive selection also matters. Preselection also adds latency before execution even when it saves tokens: from 10 to 1,000 distractors, the median routing time rises from 8 to 19 seconds for LLM preselection and from 33 to 41 seconds for hybrid preselection, which makes two LLM calls (Table 31 ). RAG needs no LLM call; because we embedded all skills and task instructions in a batch before the experiments, its preselection reduces to a similarity lookup, so we do not report a separate latency for it. Preselection is thus a useful mitigation rather than a complete solution, and its benefit must be weighed against coverage loss and response time.

sections.heading: 4.2 Results and discussion
sections.text: Skill metadata creates semantic interference. In Table 7 , masking keeps the context long, yet largely restores no-extra-skills loading (63.9% vs. 73.5% recall), cuts the zero-load rate from 62.2% to 23.6%, and is competitive with the strongest preselection row (61.1%). Because the slots and approximate length are preserved, the gain is not an artifact of a shorter context. Long metadata alone therefore does not cause routing collapse; the failure appears when distractors carry meaningful descriptions that look like plausible alternative actions.

sections.heading: Descriptions dominate the field-level effect.
sections.text: Masking only descriptions raises loaded-skill recall to 63.3%, close to full masking (63.9%; Table 8 ). Masking names or locations alone helps less (43.7% and 47.5%), and masking both together reaches only 51.7%. The latter removes the explicit targets for load_skill and direct file reads, although agents could still find the files by exploring. sections.heading: Descriptions have two functional roles.
sections.text: These results suggest a link between the two forms of interference. During execution, descriptions act as conditional sub-instructions (load this skill when its situation arises), creating a multi-instruction-following problem alongside the task. In routing-only selection, they are instead semantic-matching inputs rather than instructions to monitor. This role shift helps explain why agents select skills more reliably when selection is their sole objective, even with the full library visible.

sections.heading: 4.3 Case study
sections.text: Traces further support instruction interference. Figure 5 shows two plan-first failures. In Case 1, GLM-5 explicitly plans to load pid-controller , vehicle-dynamics , and simulation-metrics , but opens only the first. In Case 2, MiniMax M2.5 writes a step-by-step plan for a D3 visualization that mentions no skill, and never loads d3-visualization . Both runs fail. Case 1: planned but not loaded Task/model: adaptive-cruise-control , GLM-5. Agent plan excerpt: “Let me load the relevant skills first: 1. pid-controller – For implementing PID control loops; 2. vehicle-dynamics – For vehicle motion simulation and cruise control modes; 3. simulation-metrics – For calculating performance metrics.” Actually loaded: pid-controller . Missed: vehicle-dynamics , simulation-metrics , …. The run fails. Case 2: no skill plan Task/model: data-to-d3 , MiniMax M2.5. Agent plan excerpt: “Explore the input data files; set up the output directory; copy the input data; download D3.js v6; create the visualization with bubble chart and data table; add interactive features.” Actually loaded: none. Missed: d3-visualization . The run fails. Figure 5: Two trace cases under the plan-first prompt. Actually loaded counts both load_skill calls and direct reads of skill files. A prompt nudge thus does not reliably separate routing from execution; reducing the visible skill set addresses both forms of interference more directly.

sections.heading: 5 Practical Recommendations
sections.text: Because irrelevant descriptions interfere with both routing and task execution, narrowing the visible skill set before execution is more reliable than strengthening prompt instructions, and the right method depends on scale. For small curated libraries, implicit routing remains usable, but systems should track which skills are selected and loaded rather than rely on task success alone. Around the hundred-skill scale, explicit preselection should become the default; direct LLM preselection is simple and strong while the full metadata list fits in context. For thousands of skills, full-list LLM preselection becomes expensive or infeasible, and hybrid preselection (retrieval for a compact candidate set, then an LLM selector) is the strongest option in our experiments, improving relevant-skill coverage while keeping the execution context small. Since fixed preselection can omit skills needed later and adds latency, deployments should also monitor coverage and response time. Prompt reminders to consider skills are a lightweight safeguard that should complement, not replace, preselection. For evaluation, benchmarks of skill-using agents should report loaded-skill recall and zero-load rate alongside task success, since Pass@3 alone can hide routing failure.

sections.heading: LLM agents and tool choice.
sections.text: ReAct couples reasoning with actions ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , Toolformer learns tool calls ( Schick et al., 2023 ) , and MRKL combines language models with external knowledge and reasoning modules ( Karpas et al., 2022 ) . As action spaces grow, Gorilla and ToolLLM study API selection and invocation over massive API sets ( Patil et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) , MetaTool evaluates whether models know when and which tools to use ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , and RAG-MCP retrieves tools to counter prompt bloat ( Gan and Sun, 2025 ) . Overlapping tool names and descriptions also cause selection ambiguity, motivating tool merging or filtering ( Liu et al., 2025a ) .

sections.heading: Skills versus tools.
sections.text: Skills are more general than callable tools: they may package scripts or command-line workflows, but may also contain only background knowledge, constraints, procedures, or examples ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . They also enter context differently. Tools are typically exposed through callable interfaces and argument schemas ( Aizawa, 2025 ) , whereas skills use progressive disclosure: the agent first sees compact metadata, and full instructions, script arguments, or implementation details become visible only after loading ( Anthropic, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . The loading decision must therefore be made from metadata alone.

sections.heading: Reusable experience and skills.
sections.text: Voyager writes and retrieves executable code skills in Minecraft ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , Reflexion stores verbal feedback ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , and ExpeL extracts natural-language lessons from prior experience ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) . More recently, ReUseIt synthesizes reusable web workflows ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , SkillWeaver discovers and refines web-agent skills ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and SkillRL distills trajectories into hierarchical skill banks for reinforcement learning ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . These works focus on acquiring skills; we assume an existing library and ask whether agents can still route to the right skills as it grows.

sections.heading: Long-context use and retrieval.
sections.text: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves evidence before generation ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , dense passage retrieval enables scalable semantic search ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) , and Fusion-in-Decoder studies how generators consume retrieved passages ( Izacard and Grave, 2021 ) ; HyDE and Self-RAG improve retrieval with hypothetical documents or adaptive retrieval decisions ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Asai et al., 2024 ) . Long-context and needle-in-a-haystack studies show that models do not always use relevant information placed in context ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Bai et al., 2024 ; Kamradt, 2023 ) , and Du et al. (2025) find that context length alone can hurt performance even with perfect retrieval and masked irrelevant tokens. Skill routing behaves differently: replacing irrelevant metadata with placeholders largely restores golden-skill loading, so the collapse stems mainly from semantic and instruction interference rather than length alone (Section 4 ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We documented skill routing collapse: as libraries grow, agents increasingly load fewer or no skills even though the relevant skills remain available, and loading other skills instead is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only irrelevant descriptions largely restores skill loading, whereas explicitly planning skill use with the metadata intact remains less effective than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task completion. Preselection can stabilize skill use but introduces coverage and latency trade-offs. Growing skill libraries therefore call for explicit routing and for evaluating skill use, not task success alone. A natural next step is routing that revisits the selected subset during execution, recovering skills that fixed preselection omits without exposing the full library.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: For budget reasons, the proprietary-model validation covers only a 37-task subset and not every routing setting of the main study, so we treat it as a consistency check (Appendix E ). Field-level masking uses a small subset and fewer repetitions than full masking, so numerical proximity between conditions does not establish equivalence. Name-plus-location masking hides identifiers in the prompt but does not delete skill files. Embedding similarity screens plausible alternatives, not functional interchangeability. The two roles we attribute to descriptions are an interpretation of behavioral evidence, not a measurement of internal model processing. Routing latency depends on API serving conditions and does not establish end-to-end speedup; because RAG used embeddings computed in advance, our setup does not capture the cost of embedding new tasks online. Fixed preselection can omit skills needed later (Appendix J ).

sections.heading: Appendix A SkillsBench Dataset Details
sections.text: SkillsBench is a benchmark for evaluating how agent skills affect LLM-agent task solving ( Li et al., 2026 ) . The original paper describes a community-driven construction process in which 105 contributors submitted 322 candidate tasks, followed by automated checks and human review. It states that the benchmark contains 86 tasks, excludes two GPU-dependent tasks from evaluation, and evaluates 84 tasks across 11 domains. Each task is a self-contained module with a human-written instruction, a containerized environment, a reference solution, deterministic verifier scripts, and one or more curated golden skills. We use the official SkillsBench GitHub repository, which contains 87 tasks; our counts follow the repository. We exclude the five tasks in Appendix B for infrastructure or environment reliability reasons, leaving 82 adopted tasks in the main controlled study. sections.text: We measure routing-stage latency on the adopted main-study tasks with the three open-weight models across all three runs. Routing-stage latency is the time from the start of preselection until the selected metadata is passed to the executor. For hybrid preselection, it covers query generation, query embedding and retrieval, and final LLM selection, but not the one-time construction of the skill embedding index. Environment setup, task execution, and verification are excluded. P90 is the 90th percentile. The two methods were measured in separate experiment periods, so differences also reflect serving conditions. The median delay increases from 8 to 19 seconds for LLM preselection and from 33 to 41 seconds for Hybrid as distractors grow from 10 to 1,000. Hybrid preselection makes two LLM calls (query generation and final selection), whereas LLM preselection makes one. Because the two methods were run at different times, these numbers reflect the API serving conditions of each period and are not a controlled latency comparison. We do not report routing latency for RAG. It makes no generative selector call, and we embedded all skill metadata and task instructions in a single batch before running the experiments, so RAG preselection at run time reduces to a similarity lookup over precomputed vectors. Embedding calls are typically fast relative to LLM generation, but in a deployment that embeds each new task online, this step would add a small cost that our setup does not capture. Likewise, token savings need not translate into shorter end-to-end wall time, which also depends on task behavior, API latency, and environment operations. Practical deployments should weigh coverage and task success against the added routing delay, especially for interactive tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix L Prompt Templates
sections.text: This appendix gives the prompt templates. The execution agent receives skill metadata and must explicitly load a skill before using its longer instructions; preselection prompts instead return only skill names so that selected skills can be matched against the golden set.

sections.heading: L.1 Execution-agent initial prompt skeleton
sections.text: Execution-agent initial prompt skeleton ⬇ You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command - line tasks in a Linux environment . You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands . Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands . Format your response as JSON with the following structure : { " analysis ": " Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided . What do you see ? What has been accomplished ? What still needs to be done ?", " plan ": " Describe your plan for the next steps . What commands will you run and why ? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish .", " commands ": [ {" keystrokes ": " ls - la \ n ", " duration ": 0.1}, {" keystrokes ": " cd project \ n ", " duration ": 0.1} ], " task_complete ": true } Required fields : - " analysis ": Your analysis of the current situation - " plan ": Your plan for the next steps - " commands ": Array of command objects to execute Optional fields : - " task_complete ": Boolean indicating if the task is complete ( defaults to false if not present ) Command object structure : - " keystrokes ": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal ( required ) - " duration ": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete ( defaults to 1.0 if not present ) IMPORTANT : The text inside " keystrokes " will be used completely verbatim . Most bash commands should end with a newline (\ n ) to execute . — SKILL SYSTEM : If skills are available ( shown in " available_skills "), you MUST check if any skill matches the task BEFORE executing commands . Skill context : { skills_block } To load a skill , use : cat < location > ( where location is from the skill ' s < location > tag above ) LOADED SKILLS : { active_skills } To load a skill , respond with ONLY this JSON ( no other fields ): {" load_skill ": " skill - name "} After a skill is loaded , proceed with the normal response format above . sections.heading: L.2 LLM preselection prompt
sections.text: LLM preselection prompt ⬇ You are a skill - routing assistant . Given a task description and available skills , select the skills most likely to be useful . Return your answer as a JSON array of skill names . Return at most { max_skills } skills . If no skill is relevant , return an empty array : [] IMPORTANT : Return ONLY the JSON array . No explanation . No markdown code fences . ## Available Skills { skills_list } ## Task Description { task_instruction } ## Your Selection ( JSON array of skill names ) This prompt uses a strict JSON-only output format, so selected skills can be matched unambiguously and explanations are never mistaken for skill names.

sections.heading: L.3 Hybrid preselection query-generation prompt
sections.text: Hybrid preselection query-generation prompt ⬇ You are a retrieval query planner for a skill - selection system . Given a task description , write { num_queries } short search queries covering distinct capabilities likely needed for the task . Guidelines : - Each query should be concise , concrete , and skill - oriented . - Prefer capability / library / workflow phrases . - Do not restate the whole task . - Return ONLY a JSON array of strings . - No explanation . No markdown . ## Task Description { task_instruction } ## Search Queries ( JSON array ) The query-generation step is useful for multi-skill tasks because the original task instruction may emphasize the final artifact rather than every intermediate capability.

Return your answer as a JSON array of skill names . Return at most { max_skills } skills . If no skill is relevant , return an empty array : [] IMPORTANT : Return ONLY the JSON array . No explanation . No markdown code fences . ## Available Skills { skills_list } ## Task Description { task_instruction } ## Your Selection ( JSON array of skill names ) This final-selection prompt is the same as the LLM preselection prompt.

sections.heading: Appendix N Per-task Scaling Heatmaps
sections.text: The main text reports aggregate Pass@3. This appendix adds a task-level view of that metric. Figures 6 – 9 show per-task Pass@3 as the number of added irrelevant skills increases. Each row is one SkillsBench task, each column is a library-size setting, and the color encodes Pass@3 from red (all runs fail) to blue (all runs pass). The heatmaps are sorted by the Naive drop from no irrelevant skills to 1,000 irrelevant skills, so collapses under implicit routing appear near the top. This ordering makes the aggregate result more concrete: some tasks remain stable, but many tasks show abrupt failures once the library reaches hundreds or thousands of irrelevant skills. The explicit-routing heatmaps then show whether those same rows become more stable when the execution agent sees a smaller selected skill set. Figure 6: Per-task Pass@3 for Naive exposure as the number of added irrelevant skills grows. Red means all trials fail and blue means all trials pass. Rows are tasks, sorted by the naive drop from no irrelevant skills to 1,000 irrelevant skills. Figure 7: Per-task Pass@3 for LLM preselection. Compared with Naive exposure, many rows remain blue or light blue as the skill library grows, showing that explicit routing stabilizes task success when the full metadata list still fits in context. Figure 8: Per-task Pass@3 for embedding RAG. RAG is feasible at the 10k scale, but the mixed colors show that semantic retrieval alone misses some task-specific skill combinations. Figure 9: Per-task Pass@3 for hybrid preselection. The method keeps a compact candidate set while recovering more large-scale tasks than single-query RAG, especially when several capabilities must be retrieved together. Figure 6 shows the most direct form of routing collapse: rows that are blue or light blue at small scale often turn light red or red as irrelevant skills are added. Figure 7 shows the complementary result from the main text: when the full metadata list still fits, explicit LLM preselection keeps many of those rows more stable. Figures 8 and 9 focus on the scalable retrieval-based setting. RAG remains feasible at 10,000 skills but produces more mixed task-level outcomes; hybrid preselection reduces some of this variance by constructing a more diverse candidate pool before final selection.

We test whether this design scales by holding SkillsBench tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills. We find skill routing collapse : agents increasingly load fewer or no skills, even though the relevant skills remain available. With 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall falls from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%, whereas explicit selection from the same library retains 73.9% recall. Loading other skills, including plausible alternatives to golden skills, is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only the descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores skill loading, yet with the metadata intact, explicitly asking agents to plan skill use still yields lower recall than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task execution. We also evaluate explicit preselection as a practical mitigation, including its coverage and latency trade-offs. Our analysis informs skill protocols and evaluation for agents with growing skill libraries. 1 1 1 Code: https://github.com/jinlinll/lost-in-implicit-routing . 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents now operate tools and files to complete multi-step workflows in software engineering, data analysis, document processing, and personal assistance ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Such agents need reusable procedures: a plotting routine, code-audit workflow, spreadsheet operation, or domain-specific calculation should not be rediscovered in every new task. Figure 1: Lost in implicit routing. The relevant skills remain installed, but as irrelevant skills grow, agents increasingly fail to load them during implicit execution. Explicit routing recovers much of the missing skill recall. Agent skills package such procedures and their supporting resources into reusable modules ( Anthropic, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and public skill libraries are growing quickly: one analysis reports 2,179 listed skills on January 16, 2026 and 40,285 on February 5 ( Ling et al., 2026 ) . Skill selection is therefore becoming a scaling problem. We use skills to mean Anthropic’s Agent Skills, whose progressive-disclosure design works as follows: the model first sees only skill names and descriptions, and opens a full skill file only if it judges the skill relevant ( Anthropic, 2026 ) . Routing is thus not a separate stage: the agent decides whether and which skills to load while planning actions, inspecting files, and solving the task. We call this execution-time selection implicit routing . It keeps long skill files out of context, but assumes that an agent can pick out the few relevant skills from many descriptions while simultaneously solving the task. We test this assumption on SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026 ) , which provides fixed task instructions, workspaces, verifiers, and relevant skills; for each task, we keep these fixed and vary only the number of added irrelevant skills. The result is skill routing collapse : the right skills are installed, but agents increasingly load fewer skills or none at all. As irrelevant skills grow from 0 to 1,000, loaded-skill recall under implicit routing drops from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%. Agents occasionally load non-golden alternatives, but too rarely to explain the collapse. Yet the same models retain 73.9% selected-skill recall when asked only to choose skills from the full library. Relevant skills thus remain recognizable; they are lost when routing becomes a subtask of execution. End-to-end Pass@3 falls less sharply, from 51.6% to 38.6%, because strong agents can sometimes solve around missing skills; task success alone can therefore make a failing skill system look healthy. We make three contributions: • We identify and measure skill routing collapse : growing libraries make agents load fewer or no skills, rather than substitute other skills for golden ones. • We compare LLM, retrieval, and hybrid preselection on libraries of up to 10,000 added skills, and derive scale-dependent recommendations together with their token, coverage, and latency costs. • We show that irrelevant descriptions suppress skill loading and that selecting skills while solving the task makes selection less reliable, revealing semantic and instruction interference beyond context growth alone. With only 100 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall already falls by 24.6, 15.6, and 20.7 points for GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and MiniMax M2.5 (Table 2 ), while zero-load rates rise: agents increasingly stop using skills at all rather than merely choosing wrong ones. Because the slots and approximate length are preserved, the gain is not an artifact of a shorter context. Long metadata alone therefore does not cause routing collapse; the failure appears when distractors carry meaningful descriptions that look like plausible alternative actions. Descriptions dominate the field-level effect. Masking only descriptions raises loaded-skill recall to 63.3%, close to full masking (63.9%; Table 8 ). Recall is computed against the task’s golden skills. Descriptions have two functional roles. These results suggest a link between the two forms of interference. During execution, descriptions act as conditional sub-instructions (load this skill when its situation arises), creating a multi-instruction-following problem alongside the task. In routing-only selection, they are instead semantic-matching inputs rather than instructions to monitor. This role shift helps explain why agents select skills more reliably when selection is their sole objective, even with the full library visible. 4.3 Case study Traces further support instruction interference. A prompt nudge thus does not reliably separate routing from execution; reducing the visible skill set addresses both forms of interference more directly. 5 Practical Recommendations Because irrelevant descriptions interfere with both routing and task execution, narrowing the visible skill set before execution is more reliable than strengthening prompt instructions, and the right method depends on scale. For small curated libraries, implicit routing remains usable, but systems should track which skills are selected and loaded rather than rely on task success alone. Around the hundred-skill scale, explicit preselection should become the default; direct LLM preselection is simple and strong while the full metadata list fits in context. For thousands of skills, full-list LLM preselection becomes expensive or infeasible, and hybrid preselection (retrieval for a compact candidate set, then an LLM selector) is the strongest option in our experiments, improving relevant-skill coverage while keeping the execution context small. Since fixed preselection can omit skills needed later and adds latency, deployments should also monitor coverage and response time. Prompt reminders to consider skills are a lightweight safeguard that should complement, not replace, preselection. For evaluation, benchmarks of skill-using agents should report loaded-skill recall and zero-load rate alongside task success, since Pass@3 alone can hide routing failure. 6 Related Work LLM agents and tool choice. ReAct couples reasoning with actions ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , Toolformer learns tool calls ( Schick et al., 2023 ) , and MRKL combines language models with external knowledge and reasoning modules ( Karpas et al., 2022 ) . As action spaces grow, Gorilla and ToolLLM study API selection and invocation over massive API sets ( Patil et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) , MetaTool evaluates whether models know when and which tools to use ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , and RAG-MCP retrieves tools to counter prompt bloat ( Gan and Sun, 2025 ) . Overlapping tool names and descriptions also cause selection ambiguity, motivating tool merging or filtering ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Skills versus tools. Skills are more general than callable tools: they may package scripts or command-line workflows, but may also contain only background knowledge, constraints, procedures, or examples ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . They also enter context differently. Tools are typically exposed through callable interfaces and argument schemas ( Aizawa, 2025 ) , whereas skills use progressive disclosure: the agent first sees compact metadata, and full instructions, script arguments, or implementation details become visible only after loading ( Anthropic, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . The loading decision must therefore be made from metadata alone. Reusable experience and skills. Voyager writes and retrieves executable code skills in Minecraft ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , Reflexion stores verbal feedback ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , and ExpeL extracts natural-language lessons from prior experience ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) . More recently, ReUseIt synthesizes reusable web workflows ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , SkillWeaver discovers and refines web-agent skills ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and SkillRL distills trajectories into hierarchical skill banks for reinforcement learning ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . These works focus on acquiring skills; we assume an existing library and ask whether agents can still route to the right skills as it grows. Long-context use and retrieval. Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves evidence before generation ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , dense passage retrieval enables scalable semantic search ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) , and Fusion-in-Decoder studies how generators consume retrieved passages ( Izacard and Grave, 2021 ) ; HyDE and Self-RAG improve retrieval with hypothetical documents or adaptive retrieval decisions ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Asai et al., 2024 ) . Long-context and needle-in-a-haystack studies show that models do not always use relevant information placed in context ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Bai et al., 2024 ; Kamradt, 2023 ) , and Du et al. (2025) find that context length alone can hurt performance even with perfect retrieval and masked irrelevant tokens. Skill routing behaves differently: replacing irrelevant metadata with placeholders largely restores golden-skill loading, so the collapse stems mainly from semantic and instruction interference rather than length alone (Section 4 ). 7 Conclusion We documented skill routing collapse: as libraries grow, agents increasingly load fewer or no skills even though the relevant skills remain available, and loading other skills instead is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only irrelevant descriptions largely restores skill loading, whereas explicitly planning skill use with the metadata intact remains less effective than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task completion. Preselection can stabilize skill use but introduces coverage and latency trade-offs. Growing skill libraries therefore call for explicit routing and for evaluating skill use, not task success alone. A natural next step is routing that revisits the selected subset during execution, recovering skills that fixed preselection omits without exposing the full library. Limitations For budget reasons, the proprietary-model validation covers only a 37-task subset and not every routing setting of the main study, so we treat it as a consistency check (Appendix E ). Field-level masking uses a small subset and fewer repetitions than full masking, so numerical proximity between conditions does not establish equivalence. Name-plus-location masking hides identifiers in the prompt but does not delete skill files. Embedding similarity screens plausible alternatives, not functional interchangeability. The two roles we attribute to descriptions are an interpretation of behavioral evidence, not a measurement of internal model processing. Routing latency depends on API serving conditions and does not establish end-to-end speedup; because RAG used embeddings computed in advance, our setup does not capture the cost of embedding new tasks online. Appendix A SkillsBench Dataset Details SkillsBench is a benchmark for evaluating how agent skills affect LLM-agent task solving ( Li et al., 2026 ) . The original paper describes a community-driven construction process in which 105 contributors submitted 322 candidate tasks, followed by automated checks and human review. It states that the benchmark contains 86 tasks, excludes two GPU-dependent tasks from evaluation, and evaluates 84 tasks across 11 domains. Each task is a self-contained module with a human-written instruction, a containerized environment, a reference solution, deterministic verifier scripts, and one or more curated golden skills. We use the official SkillsBench GitHub repository, which contains 87 tasks; our counts follow the repository. We exclude the five tasks in Appendix B for infrastructure or environment reliability reasons, leaving 82 adopted tasks in the main controlled study.
